# Data

To test whether these hypotheses hold in the contemporary US, I combine census tract aggregates and individual data. I limit my analysis to core-based statistical areas (henceforth: metro areas) in the contiguous US with a 2024 population of at least 100.000. Tract-level data come from four non-overlapping 5-year American Community Survey (ACS) estimates (2005–2009, 2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2024; I will refer to the periods by their last year), accessed through IPUMS NHGIS. From these tract aggregates, I calculate segregation indices and other city-level aggregates for each metro area in every ACS wave. Household-level data are drawn from the corresponding ACS Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) files, accessed through IPUMS USA and limited to households residing within the same set of metro areas. Some of the metro area aggregations are based on the PUMS data.

I therefore use data with a three-level hierarchical data structure where each of the four 5-year ACS windows contains the `r length(unique(metro_vars$metro_area))` most populous metro areas in the contiguous US (therefore excluding Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and other territories) that have a population of at least 100,000 in 2024. Each metro area contains a sample of between `r min(metro_vars$n_metro)` and `r max(metro_vars$n_metro)` households in a given 5-year period (households are nested in metro areas which are nested in ACS periods). However, ACS is a repeated cross-section, not a panel. Each 5-year window within a metro area is therefore a cross-sectional sample pooled over 5 years. The total number of observations amounts to `r nrow(pums)` households.


# Housing Quality

The ACS PUMS does not collect housing quality directly. I use market-based proxies that capture both unit characteristics and neighbourhood desirability following a logic similar to hedonic price regressions. Please see the analysis for utility for the relevant analysis of hypotheses from the agent-based model for this.

- **Renters:** gross monthly rent in 1999 USD (`rentgrs_real`)
- **Owners:** self-reported home value in 1999 USD (`valueh_real`)

To remove between-metro and between-year price level differences, both measures are z-standardised within YEAR × CBSA × tenure group. The resulting `quality` variable is a within-context quality rank (mean 0, SD 1 in each group).

These measures are definitely imperfect measures of housing quality. Self-reported home values are likely biased by their owners' perception (LIT ON SUBJECTIVE PRICES?) and the rent a household pays might not be a perfect representation of market value when they have an older contract and/or the unit is under rent control. I nonetheless think that on average, higher values on these measures coincides with a higher quality/desirability of the unit. The measurement error likely attenuates the estimates though.

**Robustness check on rent control?:** In cities with rent control (notably New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles), long-term tenants may pay substantially below market rent, detaching rent from current housing quality. A robustness version of the quality variable (`quality_rc`) standardises renter quality using only households who moved into their unit within the past two years (`MOVEDIN >= year - 2`), where rents more closely reflect current market conditions.


```{r coverage}
coverage <- pums |>
  mutate(tenure = if_else(renter == 1L, "Renters", "Owners")) |>
  count(metro_name, year, tenure) |>
  arrange(metro_name, year, tenure)

summary(coverage$n)
```

The minimum group size across all CBSA × year × tenure cells is `r min(coverage$n)` households, sufficient for reliable within-group standardisation.


## Income

Household income is equivalised using the square root household size scale (`hhincome_real / sqrt(NUMPREC)`) and log-transformed to account for the well-documented diminishing returns in the income–housing relationship. The census bureau already provides income measurements adjusted for inflation (prices in 1999 USD). Households with zero or negative income are bottom-coded at 1 USD, giving a floor of log(1) = 0. Income is top-coded at the within-CBSA × year p99 to reduce the influence of extreme values.


## Housing Inequality and Population Size

```{r}
metro_vars |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  select(metro_name_short, census_region, pop_metro, gini_inc_metro, gini_rent_metro, gini_val_metro, gini_housing_metro) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("gini_"),
               names_to = "dimension",
               values_to = "gini") |>
  mutate(dimension = case_when(dimension == "gini_inc_metro" ~ "Income Gini",
                                 dimension == "gini_rent_metro" ~ "Rent Gini",
                                 dimension == "gini_val_metro" ~ "Home Value Gini",
                                 dimension == "gini_housing_metro" ~ "Housing Quality Gini")) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = log(pop_metro),
      y = gini,
      colour = dimension) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~dimension) +
  labs(x = "Log(Population)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cb_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
